passage: The first public zoo in the city of Brennan opened in 1891 with only a few dozen ______ it houses more than two thousand animals representing nearly four hundred species from six continents.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
For punctuation questions, the key test is: could each side of the blank stand alone as a full sentence?

Left side: "The first public zoo in the city of Brennan opened in 1891 with only a few dozen animals." That's a full sentence. Right side: "Today, it houses more than two thousand animals..." Also a full sentence.

Two full sentences need a period or a semicolon between them, never just a comma. Choice C uses a semicolon, plus a comma after "today," which is the usual way to set off an opening word.

rationales.A: Two full sentences joined by only a comma is called a comma splice. A comma isn't strong enough.
rationales.B: With nothing between the two full sentences, they run together.
rationales.D: This still has only a comma between two full sentences, so it's a comma splice.

passage: To make the village's traditional bread, bakers use just three simple ______ flour, water, and a sourdough starter that some families have kept alive for several generations.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
The part before the blank is a complete sentence: "bakers use just three simple ingredients." What follows names those three ingredients.

A colon is made for exactly this: after a complete sentence, it introduces a list or explanation of what was just mentioned. So choice A is right.

Think of a colon as saying "here they are."

rationales.B: A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides. The list after it isn't a sentence.
rationales.C: "Such as" already introduces the list, so adding a colon after it interrupts the phrase. Also, "such as" means examples, but this is the complete set of three.
rationales.D: Without punctuation, the list runs straight into "ingredients" and isn't set off.

passage: The museum's newest exhibit features pottery from several ancient trading ______ of the pieces were recovered by divers exploring a sunken merchant ship off the island's northern coast.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Apply the test: can each side stand alone?

"The museum's newest exhibit features pottery from several ancient trading cities." Full sentence. "Many of the pieces were recovered by divers..." Also a full sentence.

Two full sentences can be separated with a period. Choice B does that.

rationales.A: A comma alone between two full sentences is a comma splice.
rationales.C: With no punctuation, the two sentences crash into each other.
rationales.D: "And" can join two sentences, but the comma goes before "and," not after it.

passage: Tamsin Hale, a marine biologist who has studied coral reefs for two ______ spends several months each year diving off the coast of northern Australia to measure how quickly damaged reefs recover.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Strip out the extra information and see what's left. The core sentence is "Tamsin Hale spends several months each year diving..."

The phrase "a marine biologist who has studied coral reefs for two decades" is a side note about her. Side notes are fenced off by matching punctuation on both ends. This one opens with a comma after "Hale," so it must close with a comma after "decades."

Choice D closes the fence correctly.

rationales.A: A semicolon would cut the subject "Tamsin Hale" off from its verb "spends." Neither side would be a full sentence.
rationales.B: The side note opened with a comma, so it needs a closing comma too.
rationales.C: The side note opened with a comma, so it has to close with a comma, not a dash. The two ends must match.

passage: Many early telephones were sold in pairs, since there was not yet a network that could connect one telephone to many ______ a customer who wanted to talk between a home and a shop would buy two telephones and string a wire between them.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Find the two sentences hiding here. The first ends with "connect one telephone to many others." The second is "a customer who wanted to talk between a home and a shop would buy two telephones..." Both are complete.

So you need a semicolon (or period) between them. "For example" belongs to the second sentence, and like any opening phrase, it gets a comma after it.

Choice C: semicolon, then "for example," then the rest.

rationales.A: Putting "for example" between commas doesn't change the fact that only commas separate two full sentences. That's still a comma splice.
rationales.B: This is a comma splice, and it's also missing the comma after "for example."
rationales.D: With nothing before "for example," the two full sentences run together.

passage: The recipe that the chef's grandmother wrote on the back of an old envelope more than fifty years ago ______ the restaurant's most popular dessert: a lemon cake topped with candied ginger.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Sometimes the right answer is no punctuation at all. Find the subject and verb.

The subject is long: "The recipe that the chef's grandmother wrote on the back of an old envelope more than fifty years ago." Its verb is "became." And what it became is "the restaurant's most popular dessert."

Never put a comma between a subject and its verb, or between a verb and what it became. So no punctuation: choice A.

Long subjects tempt people to pause with a comma. Read it as "The recipe became the dessert" and you'll hear that it doesn't need one.

rationales.B: A comma after "became" splits the verb from what it became.
rationales.C: A colon must come after a complete sentence. "The recipe ... became" isn't complete yet.
rationales.D: A comma before "became" splits the long subject from its verb, a very common mistake.

passage: Although the bridge's original wooden planks were replaced with steel decades ______ railings, carved by local craftspeople in the 1880s, remain in place and continue to draw visitors from across the region.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
The sentence starts with "Although," which makes the first part unable to stand alone. "Although the planks were replaced with steel decades ago" leaves you waiting for more.

A dependent opening like this attaches to the main sentence with a comma. The main sentence is "the railings ... remain in place." So choice B.

Words like although, because, when and if create these dependent parts. They always need a main sentence to lean on.

rationales.A: A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides. The "Although" part can't stand alone.
rationales.C: A period would leave "Although ... decades ago" stranded as an incomplete sentence.
rationales.D: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and the "Although" part isn't one.

passage: The festival's lineup features three acts from abroad: a string quartet from Vienna, ______ a jazz trio from Montreal, Canada; and a folk singer from Lagos, Nigeria.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Look at the items in this list: "a string quartet from Vienna, Austria" and "a jazz trio from Montreal, Canada." Each item already contains a comma.

When list items have their own commas, separate the items with semicolons so the reader can tell where each one ends. The list already uses a semicolon after "Canada," so keep it consistent with a semicolon after "Austria." Choice D.

rationales.A: With a comma here, it's hard to tell where one item ends. It also clashes with the semicolon after "Canada."
rationales.B: A colon would start a brand new list in the middle of this one.
rationales.C: A dash doesn't separate list items, and it doesn't match the semicolon after "Canada."

passage: After months of negotiation, the two neighboring towns agreed to share the cost of a new water treatment ______ will serve more than forty thousand residents when it opens next year.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
"Which will serve more than forty thousand residents" can't stand alone. It's a description of the plant, and it needs to attach to the sentence about the plant.

Attach a "which" description with a comma: "a new water treatment plant, which will serve..." Choice C.

rationales.A: A semicolon needs a full sentence after it, and the "which" part isn't one.
rationales.B: A period would leave the "which" part as an incomplete sentence.
rationales.D: A colon introduces a list or explanation. Here the "which" part simply describes the plant, so a comma attaches it.
